name: Heliotherapy sunlamp

card.summary: Old-style home UV sunlamps, once sold for tanning and skin therapy, now studied mainly for their link to skin cancer.
card.note: Studies of sunbed and sunlamp use have examined melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma risk; unfiltered high-pressure bulbs can emit harmful UVC.

quick.overview:
A sunlamp is a lamp that emits ultraviolet light to tan the skin or to treat skin conditions. Early home models of the 1920s emitted a lot of UVB and were known to burn, and interest in them in looksmaxxing circles is part of the broader tan-gear category.

Today most tanning is done with beds or booths, while sunlamp-type fluorescent tubes and high-pressure bulbs survive as replacement lamps and in medical phototherapy for conditions such as psoriasis.
quick.mechanism: Low-pressure fluorescent lamps use phosphors and glass that filter out UVC, while high-pressure quartz bulbs need a dichroic filter glass to block UVC and UVB. UVA darkens existing pigment and UVB triggers new melanin production.
quick.risks: Epidemiological studies have examined sunbed and sunlamp use in relation to melanoma and skin cancers, and UV radiation is classified as a Group 1 carcinogen. Unfiltered high-pressure bulbs can emit dangerous UVC, and broken lamps release mercury.

lead: A sunlamp is an electric lamp that emits ultraviolet (UV) radiation, used for cosmetic tanning and, in clinical form, for phototherapy of skin conditions such as psoriasis, eczema and vitiligo.[1] The term heliotherapy, literally sun treatment, historically referred to using sunlight or its artificial equivalent for therapy.

Types include low-pressure fluorescent tubes and high-pressure quartz bulbs, typically rated from 250 to 2,000 watts, of which a 400-watt version has been used as a face tanner.[1] Home sunlamps of the 1920s emitted a large share of UVB and often caused burns, a problem later beds addressed by shifting output toward UVA.[2]

Epidemiological studies have examined the relationship between sunbed and sunlamp use and cutaneous malignant melanoma, and UV exposure more broadly is linked with skin cancers.[3][4][5] No published trials have tested sunlamps as an appearance intervention beyond the tan itself.

paras: Low-pressure lamps are fluorescent tubes coated with phosphors, and the glass blocks all UVC. Common sizes run from 80 to 200 watts. High-pressure bulbs are quartz and require purple dichroic filter glass to block UVC and UVB; without it they produce dangerous UVC, which is illegal in a salon setting.[1]

Older choke ballasts and newer electronic ballasts power the lamps, the latter being more efficient but costing three to five times more per lamp.[1] Output is described as peaking when the unit is between about 32 and 43 degrees Celsius.[1]
Early lamps from the 1920s were promoted as a home sun cure and emitted a large UVB share that burned the skin. Later commercial sunbeds, introduced in the late 1970s, used mostly UVA.[2]

In dermatology, a narrowband UVB fluorescent lamp emitting a peak around 311 to 312 nm (Philips TL-01) was reported in 1988 to be more effective for psoriasis than the TL-12 lamp in 10 patients, with longer tumour induction time in hairless mice.[6]

Dust blocks UV, and cleaning every 200 to 300 operating hours is described as typical. Skin oil on high-pressure bulbs can cause overheating and early failure. Broken lamps release mercury, and the page advises special precautions, especially for pregnant women.[1] Many US states restrict disposal of mercury-containing lamps.[1]

Case-control studies in the 1980s and 1990s examined sunbed and sunlamp use in relation to melanoma, including a 1990 study and a 1994 study in southern Sweden.[5][3] A 2005 study examined tanning beds, sunlamps and melanoma risk.[4] A nested case-control study in the Nurses' Health Study examined sun exposure and skin cancer risk.[7] A 1985 Montreal case-control study examined risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma.[8]

A laboratory study published in 2004 reported that UVB but not UVA radiation initiated melanoma in its experimental model.[9] A 2002 survey estimated use of indoor tanning sunlamps by US youth and their caregivers.[10]

No intervention trials of home sunlamps as an appearance treatment were found. Related human research includes case-control studies of sunbed and sunlamp use and melanoma, and a small clinical comparison of narrowband UVB lamps in 10 patients with psoriasis.[3][4][5][6]
